Biological pre-treatment: Enhancing biogas production using the highly
cellulolytic fungus Trichoderma viride
Mira Mutschlechner ⇑, Paul Illmer, Andreas Otto Wagner
Institute of Microbiology, University of Innsbruck, Technikerstraße 25d, A-6020 Innsbruck, Austria
a r t i c l e
i n f o
Article history:
Received 9 December 2014
Accepted 11 May 2015
Available online 23 May 2015
Keywords:
Trichoderma viride
Biological pre-treatment
Lignocellulose
Anaerobic digestion
Methane
Biogas
a b s t r a c t
With regard to renewable sources of energy, bioconversion of lignocellulosic biomass has long been rec-
ognized as a desirable endeavor. However, the highly heterogeneous structure of lignocellulose restricts
the exploitation of its promising potential in biogas plants. Hence, effective pre-treatment methods are
decisive prerequisites to overcome these challenges in order to improve the utilization ratio of (ligno) cel-
lulosic substrates during fermentation. In the present study, the application of Trichoderma viride in an
aerobic upstream process prior to anaerobic digestion led up to a threefold increase in the yield of
methane and total gas in a lab-scale investigation. Due to its highly efﬁcient cellulolytic activities, T. viride
seemed to be responsible for an improved nutrient availability that positively inﬂuenced the anaerobic
microbiocenosis. Aerobic pre-treatment of organic matter with T. viride is therefore a promising solution
to achieve higher methane yields and degradation performances without any additional energy demand,
nor undesired by-product inhibition.

1. Introduction
Worldwide recognition starts to prevail that the current energy
policy demands urgent replacement by more eco-conscious and
sustainable procedures. Renewable energies contribute towards
environmental compatibility, supply security, and prevention of
resource-related conﬂicts and have therefore progressively gained
global acclaim. Among potential renewable sources of energy bio-
conversion of lignocellulosic biomass has long been recognized as a
desirable endeavor (Ziemin´ ski et al., 2012; Bayer et al., 2007).
Lignocellulosic biomass refers to a highly abundant, ubiquitous
and inexhaustible source of organic matter mainly composed of
cellulose (40–50%), hemicellulose (20–40%), and lignin (5–30%)
with a worldwide production of 10–50 billion tons per annum,
accounting for about half of the global biomass yield (Pérez et al.,
2002, McKendry, 2002; Zhao et al., 2012). However, successfully
overcoming the inherent recalcitrance of lignocellulose in order
to enhance the substrate conversion is of utmost importance to
obtain high yields and high productivity indispensable to commer-
cial success (Wyman et al., 2005). Biomass recalcitrance is attribu-
table
to
the
heterogeneous
structure
and
physicochemical
complexity
of
lignocellulose
comprehensively
discussed
by
Mosier et al. (2005), Zheng et al. (2009), and Hendriks and
Zeeman
(2009).
Improvements
therefore
rely
on
efﬁcient
pre-treatment methods that alter and/or remove structural imped-
iments
to
hydrolysis,
thus
facilitating
the
accessibility
and
digestibility of (ligno) cellulosic substrates during fermentation
(Mosier et al., 2005). Current pre-treatment technologies comprise
physical, chemical, physicochemical, and biological methods (Sun
and
Cheng,
2002).
Regarding
chemical
and
physical
pre-treatment methods, inherent drawbacks such as high costs
and energy requirements, waste stream generation, and the forma-
tion of toxic by-products (e.g., weak acids, furan derivatives, and
phenolic compounds) inhibitory to the subsequent hydrolysis
and fermentation process have set barriers to industrial application
(Sun and Cheng, 2002). Biological pre-treatment, however, is
increasingly being advocated as an environmentally friendly pro-
cess with low energy input, low disposal costs, mild operating con-
ditions, and minimal by-product formation (Sun and Cheng, 2002).
Biological pre-treatment is based on enzyme initiated cascade
reactions employing (ligno) cellulolytic microorganisms, including
fungi
and
bacteria
(Dashtban
et
al.,
2009;
Chaturvedi
and
Verma, 2013). Among them, Trichoderma viride (Ascomycota,
Hypocreales, Hypocreaceae) (Chaverri and Samuels, 2003) is
known as a ubiquitous colonizer of cellulosic materials and proliﬁc
producer of a complex array of cellulose degrading enzymes com-
prising endoglucanases, cellobiohydrolases (exoglucanases), and
b-glucosidases that work in a synergistic manner (Schuster and
Schmoll, 2010; Do Vale et al., 2014). Despite prominent cellulolytic

enzymes in its secretome such as hemicellulases and pectinases
to elicit effective hydrolysis. Due to its high pH and temperature
tolerance, easy cultivability, and high level of genetic diversity
(Harman et al., 2004) T. viride and its speciﬁc multi-enzyme system
is
of
particular
interest
for
lignocellulose
pre-treatment
applications.
2. Material and methods
2.1. Cultivation of T. viride
The organism used for the preliminary experiments was iso-
lated during an investigation developing a compost starter kit
(Illmer et al., 2007) and identiﬁed as T. viride by DSMZ (Deutsche
Sammlung für Mikroorganimsen und Zellkulturen). T. viride was
cultivated on malt extract agar plates (malt extract 30 g, peptone
5 g, agar 20 g, 1000 ml distilled water, pH 6.5) at 25 C in the pre-
sent study. Cultures were preserved at 4 C for short-term mainte-
nance. For the preparation of liquid cultures a sterile malt extract
solution (malt extract 30 g, peptone 5 g, 1000 ml distilled water,
supplemented with 0.1% antifoam agent, pH 6.5) was used, inocu-
lated with the biomass extracted from three days old cultures on
malt extract agar plates, and incubated at 25 C at 150 rpm for
two days. Sporogenesis was carried out on a solid matrix according
to the procedure described in Illmer et al. (2007). During spore pro-
duction in lab scale (workload for one person 0.5–1 day) a concen-
tration of 1  107 spores g1 can be achieved within 14 days and
used to pre-treat 0.8–1.0 t of fresh bio-waste. The spores obtained
in dry powder were suspended in sterile Ringer´s solution supple-
mented with Tween 80 and used as T. viride inoculum. The viable
spore concentration in aqueous solution was assessed by cultiva-
tion on malt extract agar plates and cfu counting.
2.2. Substrate (standard bio-waste)
A mixture of organic waste representative of the average com-
position of municipal solid waste was used as initial substrate.
The composition and characteristics of the substrate used are out-
lined in Tables 1 and 2. The mixed bio-waste was chopped (target
particle size 6 2 cm), portioned, and stored frozen. Dry matter of
the bio-waste was ascertained by drying at 105 C until constant
weight was obtained. Loss on ignition analysis at 550 C was used
to determine the organic matter content.
2.3. Experimental design
Based on previous ﬁndings (Wagner et al., 2013b) the soft rot
ascomycetal fungus T. viride was used in the present study to
pre-treat the biomass samples in an aerobic upstream process
prior to anaerobic digestion. The procedure adopted aimed at
improving the substrate degradability and catabolism of organic
carbon compounds contained to achieve an increase in substrate
speciﬁc methane and total gas yield and thus a higher efﬁciency
and proﬁtability during the anaerobic bio-waste treatment. The
experimental setup was therefore divided into two parts: (i) aero-
bic pre-treatment and (ii) subsequent anaerobic digestion. With
the purpose of evaluating the impact of pre-treatment on the sub-
sequent anaerobic digestion, process-relevant parameters were
studied under varied conditions (Section 2.3.1), optimized for max-
imum methane and gas yield, and maintained at their optimized
level for further investigations.
2.3.1. Aerobic pre-treatment
Aerobic pre-treatment was carried out by inoculating 250 ml
Schott ﬂasks containing 25.0 g of the biomass samples (Table 1)
with suspended spores of T. viride. An equivalent volume of inacti-
vated spores was added to the control approaches. During aerobic
pre-treatment single parameter variation studies including inocu-
lation density, initial water content, pre-incubation period, and
composition of the substrate were performed.
In order to evaluate the impact of the initial inoculation density
during the aerobic pre-treatment process (Section 3.1), the stan-
dard bio-waste was supplemented with different amounts of
spores ranging from 2  106 to 4  108 active spores 25 g1 sub-
strate, while inactivated spores were added to the controls. The
optimum moisture during aerobic pre-treatment was investigated
by altering the moisture content of the biomass samples using dif-
ferent initial water levels (Section 3.2). With the purpose of inves-
tigating
the
impact
of
the
aerobic
pre-treatment
duration
(Section 3.3), the standard bio-waste was supplemented with
2  108 active and inactive spores, respectively, and adjusting the
moisture content to 70% before undergoing a three-day, ten-day,
and twenty-day aerobic pre-treatment. Studies focusing on the
composition of the initial substrate were carried out by inoculating
the biomass samples with 2  108 active and inactive T. viride
spores 25 g1 substrate, respectively, adjusting the moisture con-
tent to 70%, and by a two- and fourfold increase in the content of
wood (chopped wood 6 2 cm, diameter 0.5–1 cm) (Section 3.4).
During aerobic pre-treatment the Schott ﬂasks were closed with
cotton stoppers and aerobically incubated at room temperature
(22 C ± 2 C),
with
samples
regularly
taken
to
assay
car-
boxymethyl cellulase (CMCase) activity, total C and N, and the
C/N ratio. CMCase activity was quantiﬁed following the instruc-
tions of Schinner et al. (1995), total carbon and nitrogen content
was determined using a TruSpec CHN analyzer (Leco, Germany).
2.3.2. Anaerobic digestion
In the second step, the ﬂasks containing the pre-treated biomass
samples were airtight sealed with butyl rubber septa (Ochs,
Germany) and inoculated with diluted fermenter sludge (DFS)
derived from a 750.000-l biogas plant located in Roppen (Tyrol,
Austria) as described in Illmer et al. (2009). Some basic parameters
and running conditions can be found in Wagner et al. (2014). The
DFS used as inoculum in the present investigations was prepared
anaerobically as described previously (Wagner et al., 2013a). The
anaerobic incubation period extended over 14 days in total at

2.4. Statistical analysis
Statistical analysis was performed by using the Software pack-
age Statistica 9.0 (StatSoft) and SigmaPlot 12.0 (Systat Software
Inc.). Results are given as means ± standard deviation out of three
replicates. Signiﬁcant differences were ascertained by one-way or
multifactorial ANOVA. A signiﬁcance level of 0.05 was used to
assess differences between treatments. Fisher´s Least Signiﬁcant
Difference Test was used to discriminate between single variants.
3. Results and discussion
In the course of aerobic pre-treatment with T. viride, the impact
of
varied
initial
inoculation
densities,
moisture
contents,
pre-incubation periods, and compositions of the initial substrate
on the subsequent anaerobic digestion was examined as speciﬁed
in Section 2.3. The procedure adopted was conducted as a kind of
feasibility study using a lab scale approach.
3.1. Impact of varied initial inoculation densities
The application of T. viride during aerobic pre-treatment had a
signiﬁcantly positive effect on the anaerobic degradation process,
with a considerable increase in the yield of methane and total
gas in all variants supplemented with active fungal spores com-
pared to the controls (Fig. 1). At the beginning of the anaerobic
incubation period the methane yield of the individual test
approaches did not differ signiﬁcantly while presenting increas-
ingly different yields after an initial lag-phase of two days
(Fig. 1A). Within 14 days of anaerobic incubation a clear distinction
in cumulative methane and total gas production between the inoc-
ulated
and
non-inoculated
samples
could
be
observed
(Fig. 1A and B). An increase in inoculation density gradually
improved the CH4 and gas production, with the highest outputs
achieved upon using an inoculum of 2  108 T. viride spores
25 g1 substrate (Fig. 1A and B), resulting in an 88% CH4 yield
improvement compared to the controls (Fig. 1C). With a further
increase in inoculation density to 4  108 spores 25 g1 substrate
the methane and gas yield signiﬁcantly declined (Fig. 1A and B).
To enable comparison to other studies, additional data on cumula-
tive CH4 and gas production related to the organic matter content
of the substrate (in connection with experimental conditions) are
outlined in Table 3. In search of the major contributing factors
responsible for the substantial enhancement in productivity, pH
measurement did not provide any explanation since all test
approaches (± inoculation with T. viride) exhibited pH-neutral val-
ues ranging from 7.2 to 7.4 (Table 3), thus lying within the narrow
margin (pH 6.8–7.5) speciﬁed for stable methanogenesis during
anaerobic digestion (Gerardi, 2003). However, the increase in the
yield of methane and total gas in the samples supplemented with
T. viride correlated with both, a considerable increase in CMCase
activity at the end of the aerobic pre-treatment (Fig. 2A) as well
as electrical conductivity (EC) (Fig. 2B) at the end of the anaerobic
treatment. Especially the increased CMCase activity corresponding
to the gradually increasing yields of soluble, reducing sugar equiv-
alents pointed to an improved availability of nutrients, as proven
by the increase in EC (Fig. 2B) and higher microbial activities, as
assayed by DMSO reductase potentials (Fig. 2C), which peaked at

Maximum CMCase yield was achieved after ten days of aerobic
pre-treatment and again with an inoculation density of 2  108
spores 25 g1 substrate (Fig. 2A), coinciding with the signiﬁcant
increase in methane yield obtained during gas quantiﬁcation.
These results suggested that high cellulolytic activities of T. viride
during
aerobic
pre-treatment seemed
to
be
responsible
for
improved substrate conversion rates inducing a sufﬁcient nutrient
supply for the methane forming microbiocenosis, and thus reﬂect-
ing the positive inﬂuence of pre-treatment on gas yield within
anaerobic treatment. The observed yield loss after ten days of
pre-treatment and 4  108 spores 25 g1 substrate, however, might
be related to overcrowding of spores causing an inhibition of ger-
mination and development, ‘‘catabolite repression’’ of the cellulase
system or due to the depletion of macro- and micronutrients alter-
ing the fungal physiology (Nochure et al., 1993; Ghanem et al.,
2000). Another possible reason is that the high abundance of meta-
bolic active microorganisms associated with an increased total
consumption of solubilized organic matter caused the net solubi-
lization yields to cease (Fernández-Güelfo et al., 2011), resulting
in a signiﬁcant decrease in CMCase activity, electrical conductivity
as well as decreasing metabolic activities as determined by mea-
suring potential DMSO reduction (Fig. 2C). This in turn might have
caused CH4 yields to signiﬁcantly cease during the anaerobic incu-
bation in the samples supplemented with 4  108 spores 25 g1
substrate compared to those supplemented with 2  108 T. viride
spores 25 g1 substrate. In summary, the inoculation density
emerged as a decisive factor exerting a highly positive and signif-
icant impact on the overall process efﬁciency, with the highest out-
puts achieved upon using an inoculum with 2  108 active fungal
spores 25 g1 substrate, and was thus considered sufﬁcient for fur-
ther investigations.
3.2. Impact of different initial moisture contents
In accordance with the results obtained, the inoculation with T.
viride
during
aerobic
pre-treatment
once
again
exerted
a
signiﬁcant impact on the methane production rates within anaer-
obic treatment, resulting in higher methane and gas yields in all
variants supplemented with active fungal spores compared to
those without inoculation (Fig. 3A and B). Moreover, a distinct
inﬂuence of the initial water content could be observed. While
the application of T. viride during aerobic pre-treatment only
caused a marginal increase of 30% in cumulative methane genera-
tion during anaerobic treatment in the samples with a moisture
content of merely 50%, the methane yields signiﬁcantly increased
with increasing moisture level, resulting in a 50% yield improve-
ment in the samples with a moisture content of 70% and T. viride
pre-treatment compared to the yield noted in the corresponding
controls (Fig. 3C). Although a further increase in moisture level
resulted in less of an increase (33%) compared to the controls, fun-
gal pre-treatment of the biomass samples with an initial moisture
content of 90% led to the highest methane yield after 14 days of
anaerobic incubation, however, no signiﬁcant difference to the
samples with 70% moisture and T. viride pre-treatment could be
ascertained (Fig. 3C). Again neutral pH- values within a narrow
margin of 7.2–7.4 were observed at the end of the anaerobic treat-
ment, concluding that the pH level had no signiﬁcant inﬂuence on
gas yield (Table 3). Nevertheless, increasing initial moisture con-
tents showed a positive effect on CMCase activity related to
increasing yields of reducing sugar equivalents, with maximum
activities occurring in the samples with 70% and 90% moisture
and T. viride pre-treatment (Fig. 4A). Increasing moisture levels fur-
ther resulted in an increase in EC in both inoculated and
non-inoculated samples with a signiﬁcant increase in EC in the
samples with initial water contents of 70% and 90% at the end of
anaerobic incubation (Fig. 4B), which is particularly interesting
since higher water levels induce a higher degree of dilution. This
seemed to imply that T. viride initiates ion concentrations and
hence nutrient availability to increase at favorable water condi-
tions. The increase in CMCase activities along with increasing
moisture might be related to the fact that species of the genus
Trichoderma are considered as ‘‘hydrophilic fungi’’ (aw higher than

3.3. Impact of the duration of aerobic pre-incubation

of the most critical factors affecting the efﬁciency of the anaerobic
conversion performance, with methane and gas yields signiﬁcantly
increasing along with a progressive pre-incubation time of up to

pre-treatment to twenty days led to an increase in methane yield
in the controls, while it declined in the samples supplemented with
T. viride (Fig. 5A and C). Regardless of the inoculation with T. viride,
a three-day aerobic pre-treatment led to very low methane yields
achieved within anaerobic treatment (Fig. 5A). The underlying
causes were attributed to the acid pH-values observed during the
ﬁrst days of aerobic pre-treatment, which in turn led to unfavor-
able initial conditions for the subsequent anaerobic digestion.

were observed as a result of organic acid production, oxidation of
reduced sulfur and nitrogen compounds, and CO2 formed during
the initial stages of aerobic organic matter decay. The acidic condi-
tions during pre-treatment might have further affected mycelia

could be explained by the fact that low pH causes denaturation
of the enzymes and may have a regulatory effect on the adsorption
and desorption characteristics of cellulolytic enzymes. After a fort-
nightly anaerobic treatment of the three-day aerobic pre-treated
samples pH was still low (pH < 6.2) and outside the range speciﬁed

chain and disturbed degradation performance. In contrast to any
other measurements, with intermediate volatile fatty acids rapidly
being consumed, VFA quantiﬁcation in the samples that have
undergone a three-day aerobic pre-incubation revealed a buildup
and persistence of acetate and butyrate whereas propionate was
not detectable during anaerobic treatment (data not shown).
Inanc et al. (1999) reported that the formation of propionate is
suppressed at low pH, suggesting acidic conditions as the primary
cause. A buildup of acetate can, in turn, reduce the free energy
available for the anaerobic oxidation of metabolic intermediates
such as butyrate, leading to intermediate VFA accumulation
(Hickey and Switzenbaum, 1991). High VFA conditions along with
low pH are known to be inhibitory to methanogenic archaea,
resulting in a signiﬁcant decrease in metabolic activity and thus
in declining methane yield (Illmer et al., 2009). An aerobic
pre-incubation period of only three days should therefore be con-
sidered insufﬁcient due to lacking pH-stabilization, leading to
unstable conversion performance.
A ten-day aerobic pre-treatment with T. viride, however, led to a
steady and highly efﬁcient fermentation process as it was possible
to achieve an increase in pH, thus providing suitable conditions for
the subsequent anaerobic digestion. Beyond the 3rd day of aerobic
pre-treatment, pH started to rapidly increase reaching pH neutral
values after ten days of pre-incubation due to the decomposition
of organic acids, production of ammonia, and mineralization of
organic nitrogen resulting from microbial activity. The increase in

wood (Fig. 7B) and was most probably related to the persistent as
well as recalcitrant character of ligneous substrates with repercus-
sions on the milieu conditions prevailing during the process. A
principal reason is that wood based materials contain very low
contents of nitrogen, which is required to produce the enzymes
needed for sufﬁcient degradation of the main structural compo-
nents of wood – cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. While the
samples without any substrate modiﬁcation exhibited initial C/N
ratios of 22–25:1, increasing the content of wood led to higher ini-
tial C/N ratios of 35:1. In this context, Eiland et al. (2001) reported
that low initial C/N ratios caused more rapid degradation rates of
cellulose and hemicellulose (hemicellulose: 50–80%, cellulose:
40–60%), while high initial C/N ratios resulted in 10–20% degrada-
tion of both hemicellulose and cellulose. Nitrogen deﬁciency as
reﬂected by the high initial C/N ratios in the samples with
increased wood contents may therefore well have contributed to
the gradually decreasing CM-cellulase activities compared to those
where the composition of the substrate remained unmodiﬁed
(Fig. 8A). Low nitrogen substrates may also lack sufﬁcient protein
to supply the ammonia needed to neutralize acidic conditions
(Haug, 1993), which could be connected to the slight decrease in
pH observed in the samples with modiﬁed substrate compositions
(Table 3). In addition, ligneous substrates exhibit a natural acidity
of a slight-to-moderate degree, which might have also caused a
drop in pH. Increasing the content of wood further resulted in a
gradual
decrease
in
EC
(Fig.
8B)
in
both,
inoculated
and
non-inoculated samples, which could point to an inhibitory effect
of higher wood contents due to a limited excess of nutrients. In
addition to these points, wood contains natural accompanying sub-
stances such as tannins, well known for their ability to cross-link
proteins, as well as furan derivatives and phenolic compounds
formed and/or liberated during wood decay. It is therefore equally
conceivable that these substances exert a potentially inhibitory
effect on the interacting microbiocenosis during anaerobic treat-
ment and should therefore be examined further.
4. Conclusion and future prospects
Biological pre-treatment of organic matter using T. viride in an
aerobic upstream process prior to anaerobic digestion led to a sig-
niﬁcant increase in substrate speciﬁc methane and gas yield, with
single-parameter variation studies revealing optimal conditions
with an inoculation density of 2  108 spores 25 g1 substrate, an
initial moisture content of 70%, and an aerobic pre-incubation
extending over ten days in total. The improvement in overall efﬁ-
ciency was highly reproducible within test replications, and thus
a promising technique to pre-treat (ligno) cellulosic feedstock for
enhanced biogas production.
The procedure adopted harbors signiﬁcant future potential for
improving the proﬁtability of biogas plants and represents an
economically feasible process to treat domestic organic waste
as a valuable material conducive to environmentally friendly
recycling economy. The facile digestibility and conversion of lig-
nocellulosic materials based on enzyme initiated cascade reac-
tions
involving
(ligno)
cellulolytic
microorganisms
therefore
provides a signiﬁcant opportunity to improve the overall efﬁ-
ciency of energetic biomass utilization under anaerobic condi-
tions. On the basis of the insight gained in the present study,
further
investigations
shall
therefore
ultimately
contribute
towards identifying the major biochemical and microbiological
factors responsible for the sustainable productivity enhancement.
Common molecular-biological techniques are intended to provide
an insight into microbial diversity and the functional relation-
ships of the dominant phylogenetic groups, thus improving the
understanding of metabolic ﬂuxes within anaerobic treatment.
In addition, large-scale assessment shall provide the basis for
broad practical applications.
